name: Instagram 2011: Django + sharded PostgreSQL + Memcached
description: The whole architecture of Instagram one year after launch (2011: 14 million users, 3 engineers). App requests go through Route53 → Amazon ELB (SSL terminates here) → 3 NGINX servers → 25+ Django (gunicorn) servers. Most data (users, photo metadata, tags) is in sharded PostgreSQL: 12 primaries, with 12 replicas in another availability zone through streaming replication. 6 Memcached servers are in front. Redis holds the home feed, the activity feed and sessions. Geo search moved to Apache Solr. Photos go straight to S3, with CloudFront as the CDN. Sharing to Twitter/Facebook, notifying followers and feed fan-out go on a Gearman queue, and about 200 Python workers process them in the background; push notifications use pyapns. Sources: https://instagram-engineering.com/what-powers-instagram-hundreds-of-instances-dozens-of-technologies-adf2e22da2ad , https://instagram-engineering.com/sharding-ids-at-instagram-1cf5a71e5a5c . The lease approach comes from Facebook's paper Scaling Memcache at Facebook (NSDI 2013): https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi13/technical-sessions/presentation/nishtala . The parameters are small values for teaching, not Instagram's real numbers.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL (12 shards, replicas in another AZ)

notes.text: Try this: 1) Run the scenario first: at second 30 a deploy restarts 3 of the 6 Memcached servers, and they come back empty. The hit ratio falls to about 66%, every miss goes to PostgreSQL, and the shards are full; the Django threads all wait for the database. Over the run the error rate is about 7.3% and p99 about 0.85 s. Look at the per-API results in the right panel: feed and upload each fail about 13%, because they share the same database; geo search goes to Solr and does not fail, but its p99 also grows to about 0.9 s: it shares the same Django threads with feed and waits behind requests that wait for the database. Loading photos goes through CloudFront and is not affected at all. 2) Set PostgreSQL's "connections" to 2 (like a bigger pgbouncer pool, or a bigger machine): no more errors. 3) Set it back to 1 and set Memcached's stampede protection to lease: it does not help. Errors fall to about 4%, but p99 grows from 0.85 s to about 1.8 s. A lease helps when many requests ask for the "same" hot key at once; here half the cache is empty and each request asks for its own key, so requests that wait for a lease only hold threads longer.

Simplified: Django is one group of servers, and NGINX sends every request to it; Django calls different downstreams per API (each edge shows the APIs it carries). Redis is a plain service, queried on every feed read. pgbouncer, Munin, Sentry and Fabric are not drawn. The 12 shards are the number from the source; server counts and milliseconds are scaled down. How real Memcached servers warm up after a restart (for example, by sending them a small part of the traffic first) is beyond the simulator.
